utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-03-69-T, The Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. First of all, I establish that the accused are not present in the courtroom. They -- during the last hearing, they have waived their right to not be present and even expressed a wish not to be present. I do understand, nevertheless, waiver forms will be provided soon. I would say that is in addition to the waiver already expressly given and in line with the experience. I start with my agenda. First, the scope of this session. On the 30th of May, through an informal communication, the Prosecution requested a delay of this session or a deferral of dealing with issues related to personnel files. On the 31st of May, 2012, the Chamber staff informed the parties that the session would be held this week and that the Chamber would consider dealing with any issues at a later stage, if necessary. Hence, we will wait what comes up today and then see how to resolve it. Which means, Ms. Marcus, that if you shout PF, for personnel files, that is giving notice that you consider that to be a matter which you would like to be deferred and then we'll see what we will do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So PF is the code for personnel files. I move to my next item lifting confidentiality. The parties have indicated that the confidential status of the following exhibits can be lifted, and I will try to read them as slowly and clearly as possible: P1480, up to and including P1482; P3034; D374; D376; D377 [Realtime transcript read in error "D3777"]; D379; D384; D385; D390 through D392; D397; D399; D400; D401; D406; D407; D417; D419; D423 [Realtime transcript read in error "D432"]. And the same goes for the following transcript portion: Transcript page 17067, line 14, through 17069, line 5. The status of the above-mentioned is changed to public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there is a small error in the transcript. D377 appeared with one seven too much, and another one, D423 seems to appear as "D432." I take it that will be corrected and it may well be that I misspoke. Important is the accuracy of the transcript. Next item on the agenda revised translations. The parties have informed the Chamber that revised versions of Exhibits D200, D201, and D396 are available and I'm talking about translations. The Registry is hereby instructed to replace old with revised versions for these exhibits. I move to the next item: Simatovic bar table motions. On the 24th of May, 2012, the Chamber set a deadline of noon on the 4th of June, 2012, for any Defence filings seeking to tender materials for admission into evidence. On the same day in court, the Simatovic Defence indicated that it was seeking an extension of this deadline. This can be found at transcript pages 19.804 through 19.806. On the 29th of May, 2012, the Chamber informally communicated an instruction to the Simatovic Defence to file a written request by the 30th of May, 2012 and shortened the response time to noon on the 1st of June, 2012. On the 30th of May, 2012, the Simatovic Defence requested an extension of three weeks to file a final bar table motion of approximately 500 documents. The other parties did not respond. On the 1st of June, the Chamber denied the Simatovic Defence's request and informed the parties of this decision through an informal communication. Whatever was done by informal communications is, of course, hereby put on the record. In denying the request, the Chamber considered that, in relation to 350 of the documents it sought to tender, the Simatovic only identified and qualified them by referencing that they had been on its Rule 65 ter list. For a further 110 documents, the Simatovic Defence noted only that they had been selected based on the report of a dropped military expert witness. Thus, the Chamber concluded that most, if not all, of these documents had been on the Simatovic Defence's Rule 65 ter exhibit list or were otherwise known to it for a long time. The Simatovic Defence had ample opportunity during the one-year long Defence case to process and tender documents through witnesses in court or from the bar table. This year-long period included two adjournments of four weeks each granted at the request of the Defence. Thus, absent reasoned explanations to the contrary, the Chamber found that the Defence could reasonably be expected to tender any remaining documents which form a significant part of its case shortly after the end of the hearing of its last witness. Finally, in relation to the 50 documents not yet in the possession of the Defence, the Chamber considered that a party may seek to re-open its case if the legal test for such re-opening is met. On the 5th of June, 2012, the Simatovic Defence requested reconsideration or, in the alternative, certification to appeal the Chamber's decision of the 1st of June, 2012. The Chamber has now put its decision on the record and provided its reasons. The Simatovic Defence has seven days to amend its request for reconsideration or certification, if it so chooses. The Chamber instructs the Simatovic Defence to notify the Chamber and the parties if it does not seek to amend its request. The parties will have two weeks to respond from the date of this notification. I move on to my next item on the agenda which is a request for variation of protective measures. The Chamber hereby puts on the record that on the 17th of May of this year, the Stanisic Defence in an informal communication requested leave to provide the two doctors of Mr. Stanisic, for the purpose of an upcoming examination, the confidential reporting medical officer and specialist reports of the past two years. This request was granted on the 25th of May, also through an informal communication. I move to the next item on my agenda: Deferred documents from bar table decision. There were ten excerpted documents in a recent bar table decision where the chamber deferred its decision on admission. The Chamber sought further clarification on the 31st of May, 2012, but did not receive any information from the Stanisic Defence so far. Could we hear from the Stanisic Defence now? The issue being whether the whole documents of these excerpts are available to the other parties and I am referring to 1D00380, 1D00379, 1D00372, 1D01893, 1D00373, 1D00370, 1D00374, 1D00375, 1D00376, and 1D00381. Talking from my memory, these are excerpts where often just at paragraph 5 appears often. I think it's about Serbian terrorism and the question is: Are the full reports available of these and have they been disclosed to the other party?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is an issue which has arisen on many different occasions. But are they with the Defence, no. Have they been available to the Prosecution, yes, is the simple answer. Following the Rule 54 hearing in, I think, December of 2011, the Serbian government indicated that the full annual reports were available for both parties to inspect. The Serbian government was not willing to release those documents to the Prosecution or the Defence but made them available if the parties so wished to go and see them. The Defence did so. We selected the excerpts and we indicated to the Prosecution that we were only selecting excerpts and the reports were, as the Serbian government had indicated, available to the Prosecution. I'm not sure if they went to see them or not, but they are available to them and have been for five months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I have to be very careful whether we are -- these are the numbers - I have to check that - whether these are the yearly reports or whether these are the reports for shorter periods from certain -- covering certain areas - we could check that - because I think that there are two categories, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I -- I think they ought to be, I think, from the annual reports because that was what we had problems with obtaining until the Rule 54 hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me check just one ... I'm just randomly trying to find ... Yes, I see, for example, I just took one, that's paragraph 5 of that report, Serbian extremism and terrorism, for example. Ms. Marcus, would you agree that at least the Prosecution would have had access to these reports in its -- in their entirety?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I would agree with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I think we can -- we'll move on, and we'll further consider this. Then I move on to my next agenda item which is the OSCE report. The Chamber had previously asked the parties for a document that was an OSCE report which Witness Corbic mentioned during his testimony. This report -- no. I prefer, as a matter of fact, to leave this until after the first break. But the report is available. Has it been uploaded in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it has not been uploaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way you can upload it in e-court because I do understand that the report is 100 pages long, and it might be that where the Chamber was seeking to have that report in evidence, that looking at it, perhaps only smaller portions are relevant. So, therefore, is there any way that you could upload it into e-court so perhaps even during the next break we could have a look at it?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, we can do that. I send an electronic version to the Chamber's staff at his request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I have seen, as a matter of fact, that a small portion of that was on my desk, mainly the index, the table of contents. And I might want to -- the Chamber might want to have a look at it a bit closer look before we say all 100 pages are in because we are inclined to admit, and the question then remains in whole or in part, that OSCE report. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I just want to indicate for the record that we object to the filing of any of that report for very similar reasons that we object to all new evidence which is, one, that we haven't had the opportunity to deal with this report effectively through the Prosecution case and we are presuming it is going to be in support of the Prosecution case; and, secondly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Jordash, isn't there a misunderstanding. I think during the testimony of Mr. Corbic the Chamber has shown interest and invited both parties to see whether they had a copy of this report available because the Chamber would consider whether it would like to have it in evidence which is not presenting new evidence by the Prosecution but triggered by Mr. Corbic's testimony, the Chamber is considering whether or not we'd like to have that in evidence. So therefore I didn't ask the Prosecution to make any selection or -- but we -- the only thing we asked the parties, Do you have the report, could you show it to us so that the Chamber can consider whether it can use the report. Perhaps primarily also for testing the -- the credibility and reliability of the witness. So, therefore, I'm a bit surprised by your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The effect is still the same. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But are you saying Prosecution time is over now, but the Chamber's time to invite the parties to provide whatever information the Chamber would consider to seek to have in evidence and, again, I only said we are inclined to accept into evidence, it would be the Chamber exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the effect on the accused may well still be the same. It matters not whether the incriminating evidence comes in through the Prosecution's request or through the Chamber's request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether it is incriminating [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... incriminating?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I read the report and there's nothing that I can see that assists the Defence. The point is that at this stage we don't know what the Chamber wants the report for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any authority for in the case law that if a Chamber seeks to have something in evidence, even if the Chamber, at that moment, is neutral on whether it supports a Defence witness or whether it challenges the -- that the Chamber would be -- would not be in a position to seek that evidence at any stage of the proceedings? Even if the effect -- again, I do not know what the effect is. Apparently you know better. Is there any authority for this position? I thought, as a matter of fact, that your initial objection was against the Prosecution now providing evidence which they should not do at this stage anymore. I explained to you that that is in my view not the situation. Do you have any authority for the Chamber being barred after the Prosecution's case to seek any evidence which may or may not be disfavourable to the accused? What about Chamber witnesses? What is their -- are we not allowed to hear the evidence of Chamber witnesses if there is a possibility that it might be disfavourable to the accused? I'm seeking any authority for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There is no authority for it, and there is no authority against it either. The position, as far as I'm aware, is that the Defence has a fundamental right to be able to challenge evidence which is used to convict him. That's the authority that I rely upon, and there's a huge body of jurisprudence in support of that. But I'm not going to press the point. If Your Honours consider that it is fair to call evidence which is, in the end, to be used to incriminate the accused without the accused having an opportunity to rebut that evidence, then I'm not going to press the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you asked for an opportunity to rebut that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's what I was doing just then, why I was indicating an objection to the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But seeking an opportunity to rebut evidence or to object against admission, because admission in itself would be unfair anyhow, is not the same isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The first step is to object to the evidence and then I don't need to seek to rebut it. The second step is if Your Honour admits it then we would appreciate an opportunity to know the potential use for that evidence and then consider our position as to whether we apply to the Chamber to -- to -- to call evidence to rebut that evidence. And that, in my submission, is a general principle which applies to all of the Chamber's potential witnesses or evidence that the Chamber decides it's going to call after the parties have called their case. That, in my submission, is a basic principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not there. The Chamber first would like to have it uploaded in case it would seek to have it in evidence as a Chamber exhibit. And we'd first like to have a look at it. But I do understand, and I should have known, as a matter of fact, I saw the table of contents this morning, so must be somewhere. Thank you. But if it could be uploaded, and if it's needed that it's there. Thank you, Ms. Harbour and Mr. Jordash. Then next on my agenda is that should read a statement on the admissibility of redacted documents marked for identification. I'll deliver this statement from the Chamber on the admissibility of redacted documents marked for identification. During the housekeeping session of the 28th of March of this year, the Chamber instructed the parties to express their views on the admission of two categories of documents that are currently marked for identification: One, documents containing redactions; and, two, documents received from the accused. The Chamber's staff distributed a sample format for these joint submissions to the parties. On the 11th of April, the parties filed a joint submission regarding documents marked for identification that have redactions or whose provenance is unknown. The parties explained that the second category of documents was modified to reflect the reality that not all documents missing provenance information necessarily came from the accused. On the 16th of April, the Stanisic Defence filed an addendum to the joint submission. And on the 23rd of April the Prosecution filed a request to reply to the Stanisic defence addendum, attaching its reply to the request. On the 26th of April, through an informal communication the Chamber granted leave to reply -- leave to the Prosecution to file a reply and accepted the attachment to the request as the reply. The Chamber will address the second category of documents marked for identification received from the accused or whose provenance is unknown in a separate statement. The Chamber starts by noting that there are no longer any objections to the admission of documents D456, D462, and P3063. I would like to hear from the Simatovic Defence whether the revised translations of D456, D462, and P3063 have been uploaded. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Your Honours, please. Your Honour, I believe the translation do exist. As far as I can ... yes, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are the revised translations?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these are translations as received from the translation service. Now I really cannot say whether they are revised or not, but there was a problem with those documents; for example, for D456. A response was awaited from the Prosecution that was clarified in the meantime. I do not have anything noted here that there was a problem with the translation. Perhaps that's our mistake. I apologise in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that I might have made a mistake that it was just a matter of translations being available and not revision of translations. Ms. Harbour, is that what you can confirm?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The issue with D462, as we left it at the last housekeeping session, was an issue of the translation being available, and I wanted to clarify whether your request or your question about revised translations pertained to translations of the unredacted files. And if that is the case, I don't think we're -- we have quite gotten there yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll deal with this one after the break so that I have another opportunity to check. From what I just learned, is that it was -- the translation had to be revised because of the original now being unredacted. Is that correct? But we'll deal with it after the break. I'll just make a note.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: When we do get to dealing with the issues with the redacted and unredacted files, I have a brief background that I would like to make -- background submissions that I would like to make to just give everyone an overview of some of the issues that we've encountered which I think will make it go smoothly if we -- if I give those before we launch into discussions of specific documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, would you suggest to do it now?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: If Your Honour would wish, that would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps that would be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: As we indicated in our informal e-mail of the 30th of May, we've encountered a number of unexpected hurdles in processing the unredacted JSO files. And to ensure that replacing admitted portions of the redacts files with unredacted files in e-court would go smoothly, we've tried to address these hurdles. But, just as a quick summary, the scans we received from Serbia for this batch of documents were of much lower quality than the batch that we received with redactions and the batch that had been tendered into evidence with the redactions. They're much harder to read. Many pages are upside down or side ways, and several of the files were received in a different order than the files previously received and the files that are in evidence. There are also a few -- a small number of substantive differences in the files; namely, on some occasions, the files included an extra page or two, and in some instances isolated documents from one individual's file were located in someone else's file. To deal with some of the technical issues, we printed and scanned the documents to process them rather than processing the digit images and having the digital images stamped. After this process was complete we determined that in some cases this process had decreased the legibility and pages that were legible in the digital form had become illegible. In an attempt to protect the legibility of the pages that are legible in the digital form, we're working with our evidence unit to reprocess some of these files. We've redoubled our efforts to resolve any outstanding technical and administrative efforts with respect to these files and we have been able to resolve most, but not all, of the issues that impact the MFIs for today's housekeeping session. And because of the issues inherent in the documents received we're going to suggest that instead of replacing the redacted documents with the unredacted documents in evidence, as I think all of the parties and the Chamber had originally anticipated, we're going to suggest that we keep the redacted files in evidence and introduce as a separate exhibit either the entire unredacted file or the pages from an unredacted file that correspond to redacted pages and the redacted file. There are several benefits of this which can I discuss in greater deal when we talk about specific documents but one of them is that all of the redacted files can be public. Some have been tendered as confidential exhibits out of an abundance of caution, but we've now verified that they can be public; whereas the unredacted files can not be. So this will result in us effectively having a public redacted version of these files. And, in addition, this will protect the evidentiary value of the documents and protect the evidentiary record where certain page numbers were referred to on the record that may be different now or where certain pages may not be legible in the unredacted files that are legible in the redacted files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Harbour. Any need to add anything to that, Mr. Petrovic, or Mr. Jordash? Now in the beginning no one was on his feet, now you both are.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'd like to, if I may, just very briefly. I have listened to what the Prosecution have just said with a great deal of concern. The issue as presented by the Prosecution as an administrative one but is plainly not an administrative one, because the contents of those so-called personnel files may well go to the heart of the case against the accused. If at one stage, and if I understand this correctly this is what the Prosecution are saying, one stage they receive a so-called personnel files with certain documents contained within it. Now they receive the -- the -- the same so-called personnel files but with other documents in it, both from the same source: The Serbian government, via, according to the Prosecution, BIA. So what we have now is the Prosecution attempting to reconcile that problem as an administrative problem when, in fact, it is a forensic problem because they present these personnel files to you, the Court, as an accurate reflection of a factual and legal scenario; i.e., this is the personnel files belonging to X, you can be satisfied that these documents were in this file and these reflect a member of a special unit which was supervised by the accused. They then receive a personnel file with different documents and instead of presenting evidence which clarifies why this later file has different documents, they set their evidence unit to sorting out the disparity or discrepancy. In our submission, that is not really satisfactory. We have complained throughout this trial that these are not personnel files, first of all; secondly, we put forward to the Court that these files may well have been tampered with. In fact, from the first accused's perspective have certainly been tampered with. At the close of the case, the Prosecution present this situation which, in our submission, goes to the heart of those issues. And just, if I may just complete this submission, if these issues had been before the Court at the beginning of the case, if the personnel files had been presented as part of the Prosecution case, these are the types of issues which the Defence would had a chance to challenge, adjudicate, or have adjudicated, call evidence concerning the contents of these files, and so on. We've been deprived of that opportunity. And this situation now presented by the Prosecution is another prejudice to the Defence which we cannot, at this stage, remedy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it was my understanding, but please correct me whether I'm wrong, Ms. Harbour, when you sought to be provided with unredacted versions of documents you had, that you then received not only the unredacted versions apart from how legible and whether electronic or not, but that sometimes even other elements were added to that. Is it your intention to remove anything that you received in addition to what you had and what you sought to be provided in an unredacted form so as not to add anything to what you sought to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. That is the -- absolutely the intention. On very few occasions there were substantive differences, an extra page or a page misplaced in a file, on very few occasions. And certainly when we upload and tender, or if Your Honour would allow for an additional exhibit, we would not include any documents that do not match exactly with the documents that are currently in evidence. However, there is still a very kind of widespread issue of ordering. Many of the page numbers are out of order. So while the pages for the most part are the same pages they are not in the same order, which is one technical issue. And another issue that I would just like to point out is that all of these documents have been disclosed to the Defence and, of course, they are more than welcome, and I would even perhaps encourage them to do a comparison of any unredacted versions of redacted files that are currently in evidence to make sure they are satisfied that it is the exact same evidence with the exception of the redactions removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so to that extent, Mr. Jordash, where you were afraid that anything would be added, apart from the fundamental discussion you have raised not for the first time, but if now in this new round of receiving unredacted documents if anything would be extra, not asked for, if I understand you well, that -- that will be discarded anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, there's two problems, as I see it. The first problem is this: Which is the correct file? The one that the Prosecution received earlier on in the proceedings or the one that the Prosecution received now, with the additional documents in it? On what basis do the Prosecution say that the first file received and tendered is one that Your Honours should rely upon as reflecting the personnel file in relation to that particular individual. The second problem, as I see it, is that we don't know and the Court doesn't know the difference between the first and the second because the Prosecution's evidence unit is resolving the discrepancy behind closed doors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that everything you received legible or not legible, electronic or not electronic, that you have disclosed that to the Defence, so that if this raises an issue as to whether the personnel file -- to the -- to the documents which we were presented with as the personnel file that if now the unredacted version suddenly raises entirely new questions: Is this the personnel file or is a forgery or is there -- that at least the Defence has an opportunity at this moment to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry for interrupting. Yes, everything has been disclosed. And, in addition, I would like to correct the record. Our evidence unit is certain not manipulating evidence in any way. When I referred to the evidence unit, I simply referred to restamping the documents, hopefully in a more legible form. They're not changing the order which is why we end up with some order issues. We are rotating pages and trying to -- we are rotating pages when they were given to us upside down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you'd say you are saving, as a matter of fact, musculature of Mr. Jordash. It's a--

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Exactly, we're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: We're preserving errors that may have been in the documents that -- received from Serbia because that's how they were received.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I understood the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps a cup of tea or a cup of coffee so that you understand exactly what Ms. Harbour says the evidence unit is doing at this moment. And then see what problem then remains. Because, may I take it, Mr. Jordash, that you would have no strong objections against having to turn your head for every next page to read it; that that is not something that is worrying you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It -- I -- I -- I'm not suggesting that the evidence unit manipulated and I haven't suggested that. But as I understood it, the Prosecution were saying that they were reconciling the second version of the file by ensuring it was the same as the first version of the file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there's -- of course, there's an inherent problem. If we have a document consisting of five pages with some redactions here and there, and if the Chamber says, We would like to have those documents in an unredacted form, and then you receive seven pages, although the redactions removed, what I do understand what you are doing is to identify which are the five pages which were in unredacted form first, and then remove the others, but giving Mr. Jordash, providing him with all seven pages, a full opportunity to check whether those two extra pages raise any issue as to authenticity of the original five that were presented to the Chamber. Is that how I have to understand the reconciling exercise?

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honour, our evidence unit is not conducting any of this reconciling evidence -- or, exercise. They are simply stamping the evidence in the way that it was received. And if there are extra pages, there are extra pages. And those documents go into our system as received. When I proposed removing the documents, I was referring to the process of us as the Prosecution team on this case removing those before uploading them into e-court so that the unredacted file would match the redacted file in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you would then discuss with Mr. Jordash over a cup of cafe or a cup of tea would be, Look, Mr. Jordash, for this document we received more and we are inclined to remove the extra pages so that Mr. Jordash if it raises any concern could say, Well, don't do that, I would prefer to have them in addition to the ones already in. But this is not a matter we should, I think, at this moment take any further in this -- in this session because you first have to look at it and Mr. Jordash must have an opportunity to see what are you doing and to understand what you are doing. I think I understood most of it but perhaps not fully, but the first one we should understand. Yes, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We would appreciate a statement from the Prosecution saying what the difference is because -- and the reason I'm putting it in this way is that the sooner we know, the sooner we, the Defence, will know whether we need to investigate what has happened here. Because if there is evidence that the files even at this stage are being altered, and I put it neutrally, that goes to the Defence position that the files are being stored in a place where they can be altered. And so if the Prosecution can put together a brief statement saying, These are the discrepancies in terms of addition or admitted documents, we are one step forward and can make that decision and time is, of course, of the essence.

utterances.text: -- and not the old version.

utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, would you please attach the English translation. And then D291 is admitted in evidence. Any need to have it under seal? utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I move on. D356. Prosecution no longer objects to admission, at least not on the ground of redactions in that document but, still, challenges the authenticity. utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D357 [sic]. Moving to D464 the Chamber notes that this document does not contain any redactions and we'll therefore decide on this document separately. And this concludes the statement in relation to the admissibility of redacted documents which were marked for identification. I move onto the next item on the agenda, which is MFIs with provenance concerns. The Chamber will now deliver its statement on the admissibility of documents marked for identification which were obtained from the accused or whose provenance is unknown and, to the extent possible, its decisions on the admission of specific documents. During the housekeeping of the 28th of March of this year, the Chamber instructed the parties to express their views on the admission of two categories of documents that are currently marked for identification: One, documents containing redactions; and, two, documents received from the accused. A sample format for these joint submissions was distributed to the parties by the Chamber's staff. On the 11th of April, the parties filed a joint submission regarding documents marked for identification that have redactions or whose provenance is unknown. On the 16th of April, 2012, the Stanisic Defence filed an addendum to the joint submission, and on the 23rd of April the Prosecution filed a request to reply to the Stanisic Defence addendum attaching its reply to the request. Until now, the report is the same as for the previous statement. On the 26th of April, through an informal communication, the Chamber granted leave for the Prosecution to file a reply and accepted the attachment to the request as the reply. The Chamber reiterates at the outset that it has brought discretion under Rule 89(C) in determining the admissibility of evidence. The fact alone that a document was obtained from the accused or has not been authenticated by the National Council will not necessarily render it admissible. Evidence need only exhibit sufficient -- the evidence need only exhibit sufficient indicia of reliability to be admissible. The Chamber may deem a document to have probative value on the basis of inherent properties of the document, such as its appearance, including stamps, format or signatures and/or the content of the document, and/or the existence of related evidence, including evidence corroborating the content or the format of that document. However, the admission into evidence does not, at this stage of the case, in any way constitute a final and binding determination as to the authenticity or trustworthiness of the documents sought to be admitted. Such factors are to be considered at the later stage in the case when the Chamber evaluates the probative weight to be attached to this evidence in the context of the entirety of the case. The Chamber will address each of the MFIs with provenance concerns in turn. Start with D757. This document was addressed in the Chamber's seventh decision on the Stanisic Defence bar table motion of the 17th of February, 2012, a decision which was filed yesterday, the 6th of June. D293, this document was admitted into evidence on the 30th of May during the testimony of Defence witness Radivoje Micic. D784, the Prosecution withdrew its objection to this document on the 31st of May of this year. The Chamber, therefore, admits into evidence D784. Madam Registrar, could you assist me in knowing whether there's a need to have it admitted under seal. There's no need to have it under seal. D508. The Prosecution does not object to D508 given its uncontroversial nature and indicia of reliability. Therefore, D508 is admitted into evidence but under seal. I move to D696 and D697. The Prosecution withdraws its objection to these documents, in light of the National Council's representation that it has records thereof. The Prosecution further notes that the documents appear to bear official stamps and signatures. The Prosecution requests, however, that the handwritten notes in the document should be disregarded. The Defence does not oppose this request. The Chamber therefore admits D696 and D697 into evidence but will disregard the handwritten notes contained therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I move to D56, marked not admitted. While Defence witness DST-34 identified the stamp on this document as that of the Federal Secretariat of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, and the signature as that of the federal secretary of the interior, Petar Gacanin, the National Council has indicated that it is not in possession of the document. Despite the prima facia indicia of reliability on the face of the document, the National Council's response weighs heavily against its authenticity, and the Chamber therefore denies the admission of this document. I move to P3080. The Chamber observes that this document lacks any official stamp or marking. Defence witness, Gvozden Gagic recognised some of the names in the list but did not confirm that there were, in fact, suspended from the police force. Before I move on, I'd like to inquire with the parties whether any response has been received from the National Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider during the break whether it would already decide, which would mean under the present circumstances non-admission because of late request for verification.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will not wait until after the break. This failure to seek in a timely way the position of the National Council leads the Chamber to deny the admission of P3080. I move onto D304, D305, D306, D308, D309, D310 and D311. The Chamber observes that these documents lack official stamps or markings. Only three of the documents appear to identify their authors. While Defence witness DST-034 provided some but generalised observations about these documents, he did not authenticate them. The Chamber is aware that there was a pending request for authentication with the National Council. Any result from that request? No response.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We asked them to respond by the 4th of June, but we received no -- no response so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then under those circumstances, the Chamber denies admission for lack of sufficient indicia of reliability. Therefore, it's now marked, not admitted. D330. This is a document which describes the general conditions faced by Serbs in Croatia. The Chamber observes that this document lacks official stamps or markings and its author is unknown. While Defence witness DST-043 confirmed the contents of this document, he did not authenticate it. There is a pending request for authentification. Any result?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The same as the previous one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber, also in relation to D330, denies admission for lack of sufficient indicia of reliability. I move on to D362, documents signed by an individual who appears to have been killed in 1994. While Defence witness Nebojsa Begorevic [phoen] addressed this document, he did not authenticate it. There is a pending request for authentification. Any results from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Same as before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the decision is that the Chamber denies admission for the lack of sufficient indicia of reliability. D365. This appears to be a reproduction of a TO instruction in a book. There is a pending request for authentification with the National Council. The Prosecution has further stated that this document was obtained from one of its then-perspective witnesses. When Defence witness Nebojsa Begorevic was shown this document, he stated that he was unsure of having received this TO instruction. Is there any further knowledge of the provenance of this document available to the parties, particularly, for example, about the book in which it was reproduced? And, of course, another question would be whether the National Council would have responded to a -- any request or given any information.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the moment I don't have any further information, but if the Chamber would like us to, the Prosecution would be happy to look into this matter further and see if we can provide any further information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would that take? Because I do understand that you received it from one of your perspective witnesses who then apparently was not called to testify. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: That's my note as well, Your Honour. I don't have personal knowledge of who that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then, you're closer to this Tribunal at this moment than the National Council, so perhaps matters could be resolved during the break, and that's a different situation. Under those circumstances, we'll not yet decide on the admission of D365. But we'd like to hear from you after the break, or after the next break. I move onto D394. The Chamber recalls that Defence witness Milenko Lemicic's opinion was that this is an authenticate SDB document, although he was unfamiliar with its contents. The document does not contain any official stampings or signatures and there are various handwritten notes and marks therein. There is a pending request for authentication with the National Council. Any response received?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No response received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Despite a lack of response by the National Council, the Chamber admits D394 into evidence. The Chamber has considered that this document bears sufficient indicia of reliability for it to be admissible, particularly in light of Defence witness Milenko Lemicic's testimony in relation thereto. D394 is admitted into evidence, under seal. I move onto D425. The Chamber notes that the original B/C/S document of D425 is identical to 1D02416, which is subject of the Stanisic Defence bar table motion, albeit with a slightly different English translation. 1D02416 is therefore deemed withdrawn from the bar table motion, and we'll deal with it in relation to D425. Defence witness Radenko Novakovic stated that he saw this document for the first time and considered that this document was probably written by the analytical administration and found it to be an excellent analysis of the VJ. The document lacks any official stamps and it does not contain a copy number. There is a pending request for authentication with the National Council. Any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber denies admission for lack of sufficient indicia of reliability. The status of D425 is therefore marked not admitted. D689, a document which describes the socio-political situation in the area of Vukovar. The Chamber notes that this document bears no stamps indicating that it is an official state security report. Defence witness Aco Draca was questioned regarding the second paragraph of this document, and he agreed that this paragraph was accurate. He was not asked to authenticate the document however. There is a pending request for authentication with the National Council. Any response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D689 is -- admission is denied for lack of sufficient indicia of reliability. I move onto D357. This document does not bear any official stamps or signatures. Furthermore Defence witnesses Radenko Novakovic and Jovan Dimitrijevic were questioned on this document but had no knowledge thereof. Moreover, the National Council has indicated that it is not in possession of this document. The response of the National Council and the lack of other indicia of reliability weigh heavily against the document's authenticity. D357 is therefore denied admission. D366. This document contains an order of Lieutenant-General Tomislav Simovic to Martic and Kojic to implement a cease-fires on the 18th of September, 1991. It appears to bear official stamps. Defence witness Dusan Knezevic confirmed that such a cease-fire did take place. The Stanisic Defence indicated that it would lodge a request for authentication with the National Council. Has such a request been made, and is there any response to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: A request has been made and is outstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Despite the lack of a response by the National Council, the Chamber considers that the document bears sufficient indicia of reliability and therefore admits D366 into evidence. D535. This document is unsigned and bears no stamps indicating either transmission or receipt. Has there been any response from the National Council?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This document which is said to be a letter from the accused Stanisic but is unsigned and bears no stamps indicating either transmission or receipt, the Chamber considers that it lacks sufficient indicia of reliability to be admitted. The Chamber, therefore, instructs the Registry to mark D535 as not admitted. D748, 749, 750 and 751. The parties have not indicated whether a request for authentication is pending with the National Council in relation to these documents. When presented with D748, Defence witness Mladen Karan commented that that was the first time he had seen it. He was not questioned, however, on D749, 750, and 751. The Chamber notes that the documents lack any stamps or indication of authorship. D749 is alleged to be an intercept of a conversation between two BiH army officers. The document indicates that there were reception difficulties resulting in the non-transcription of portions of the intercepted conversation. D750 further lacks an English translation, and both D750 and D751 contain handwritten notations. The Chamber further notes, however, that D749 appears to be from a publication of the third department of the 7th Administration and not from the 8th Administration, as the joint submission indicates, but -- this is what the Chamber observed. Based on this, that is, that D749 appears to be from a 7th Administration publication, the Chamber considers that this document bears sufficient indicia of reliability to be admissible and admitted D749 into evidence. The Chamber, however, denies admission of D748, D750, and D751 for lack of sufficient indicia of reliability. I suggest to the parties that we take a break first and that we resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I revisit a few matters we dealt with before the break. But, Ms. Marcus, you're on your feet.

utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave I'd like to just put one thing very briefly on the record. The one additional thing that will be done which is appropriate in our understanding, according to the protocol, is flipping the upside down pages, just spinning them. That's it. So if Mr. Jordash would like to have a copy of the digital version on a CD as received we can provide that to him immediately, if that would be of assistance. That is what's happening with the evidence unit. Okay. Completely apart from that, we have some files admitted, some parts of files, some documents from files and much of that is some of those pages were admitted redacted, as we all know. We will be able to give specific information to the Chamber, hopefully some today, but maybe not all today, with respect to those documents that are in issue in this trial, not with respect to the whole collection. I just wanted to make sure that we didn't confuse the evidence processing aspect with what the Prosecution team is doing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm -- in -- in the dark. Perhaps it's me, but the -- the sole issue is whether later files -- different in composition to the earlier files. utterances.text: One second.

On the 8th of November [sic] of this year the Stanisic Defence filed a motion seeking an order, pursuant to Rule 54 of the Tribunal's Rules, to compel the Prosecution to produce the military notebooks written by General Ratko Mladic, for the purpose of using them in court during the testimony of expert Witness Browne. On 15th of March, the Chamber decided to deny the motion to compel and informed the parties through an informal communication to be put on the record at a later stage, as is done by now. In reaching its decision, the Chamber considered that the Stanisic Defence sought, and was given, access to inspect and examine the original notebooks through expert Witness Browne. These examinations were documented in the Browne expert report. The Chamber also considered that the expert Witness Browne was called pursuant to Rule 94 bis(B)(ii) of the Rules to be cross-examined by the Prosecution. In this respect, the Prosecution's wish to cross-examine the expert did not indicate any need to have the notebooks produced in court, as the purpose was to challenge the conclusions contained in the Browne expert report. The Prosecution did not dispute the physical condition of the notebooks. Furthermore, the Chamber considered that its personal observation of the notebooks would not assist it in better understanding expert Witness Browne's testimony or his expert report. The Chamber considered that the observations of the physical condition of the notebooks and the conclusions based thereupon, which are contained in the Browne expert report, were easily comprehended by the Chamber's review of the expert report itself or would be through expert Witness Browne's testimony. Finally, the Chamber considered that should it have determined a need to physically observe the notebooks during or after expert Witness Browne's testimony, the Chamber retained the right to reconsider and to order, proprio motu, pursuant to Rule 54 the production of the notebooks for the Chamber to inspect them. The decision on the motion is hereby put on the record, including the reasons. If I said, which is possible in the beginning, that the motion was filed on the 8th of November, then it has been a mistake, because the motion was filed on the 8th of February. Just to make that clear: That the decision was, on that motion, filed the 8th of February, 2012. As a preliminary matter, the Chamber notes that the Stanisic Defence requested a written decision. The Chamber considers that the parties have an equal possibility to request certification to appeal or reconsideration of any Chamber decision, without distinction, as to whether that decision is an oral decision or a decision in writing. The Chamber sees no particular rationale for this request; therefore, opts to issue an oral decision on this matter. In its submissions, the Stanisic Defence argues that it has not been provided with consistent notice of the Prosecution's case with respect to the Mladic notebooks. In particular, the Stanisic Defence submits that the Prosecution's position is unclear and has shifted throughout this case in relation to whether the notebooks were contemporaneously written, whether they have in any way been altered or had portions removed, and as to how and by whom the notebooks have been damaged. Given that excerpts of the notebooks have been admitted into evidence and that Mr. Mladic is listed as a member in the alleged joint criminal enterprise with Mr. Stanisic, the Stanisic Defence submits that the Prosecution should identify with precision its position in relation to the notebooks in order to ensure a fair trial and the proper administration of justice. In its response filed on the 19th of April, 2012, the Prosecution requests that the Chamber deny the motion. The Prosecution submits that its position in relation to the notebooks has not shifted and that there is no legal obligation for it to provide its position in relation to a theory advanced by the Stanisic Defence as a part of its case. The Chamber recall its decisions of the 10th and 11th of March, 2011, in which it found each admitted excerpt of the notebooks to be relevant and deemed them to have probative value to the present case. It further recalls that the Prosecution met the requirement that it, and I quote: "Be able to demonstrate, with clarity and specificity, where and how each document fits into its case." In relation specifically to the contemporaneous nature of the notebooks, the Chamber recalled that in its 10th of March, 2011, decision, it stated that it, and I quote again: "Will cautiously and continuously assess all evidence that comes before it that may contradict the apparent contemporaneous nature of the notebooks." Further, the Chamber notes that it is the Stanisic Defence's case that the notebooks are unreliable and that they were not contemporaneously written, have been altered to implicate Mr. Stanisic and/or have had portions omitted. In this respect, the Chamber also notes that the Stanisic Defence did not raise arguments as to reliability, or file a response at all, to the Prosecution's motion for the admission of the notebook decided upon in the Chamber's decisions of 10th and 11th of March, 2011. After careful consideration of the parties' submissions, prior motions and the trial transcript, the Chamber does not find that the Prosecution's position is either unclear or that it has shifted in relation to the notebooks. The Chamber considers that the Prosecution is not obligated to indicate its position regards the Stanisic Defence theory or interpretation of evidence discovered only after the start of the trial. In this same respect, the Prosecution is not obligated to indicate its view on the Stanisic's Defence's exploration of the circumstances surrounding the search and the seizure of the notebooks. In relation to ensuring a fair trial, the Prosecution's trial strategy of whether and how to respond to the Defence's case does not inhibit the Defence from pursuing its theory of the case or impact its ability to present evidence in support thereof. Finally, the Chamber will continue to carefully consider all evidence put before it, by all parties, in relation to the notebooks. And the Chamber, therefore, denies the Defence motion. If, in the comment, there is substance which is not commenting on the document but is independent from the document to be considered as relevant evidence, the Chamber may use that but we'll disregard any comment which comments on the document. Is that clear to everyone? Unless there's any extremely urgent matter to be raised now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. It's only the question of the request to extend the response time to the bar table motions. If -- I have a very brief oral submission or I'm happy to file it or send it by e-mail as Your Honour prefers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I prefer it to be sent by e-mail. Members of the Chamber have commitments elsewhere and therefore would not want to go over the usual time. And if the Chamber has made up its mind on the matter or if the Defence wants to further respond to that, then we would like -- would it be possible to receive any responses by tomorrow, noon? Would that be -- if it is immediately now sent by e-mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so if there is any need to further response to what will be sent by e-mail by Ms. Marcus this afternoon, we will put everything on the record at a later stage, we expect a brief response by tomorrow noon. If there are no other matters at this moment which we urgently have to address, we adjourn for the day and we'll resume on Tuesday, the 12th of June, and now -- I think I said 3.00. And that, most likely, will be in this same courtroom, II. We stand adjourned.
